2026 Asian Games: Japan. Nagoya will be the third Japanese city to host the Asian Games, after Tokyo in 1958 and Hiroshima in 1994.

Roman Republic: Latin. Its political organisation developed at around the same time as direct democracy in ancient Greece, with collective and annual magistracies, overseen by a senate.

Joseon: Korean. It was founded by Taejo of Joseon in 1392 and replaced by the Korean Empire in 1897.

Which country used the assignat as its official currency?

Alan Bean (March 15, 1932 - May 26, 2018) was an American naval officer and aviator, aeronautical engineer, test pilot, NASA astronaut and painter.
United around 3150 BC by a ruler called Menes or Narmer, this Nile-valley civilization is considered one of the world's cradles of civilization — name it?
Ancient Egypt was a cradle of civilization concentrated along the lower reaches of the Nile River in the northeastern corner of Africa.
This Greek god of medicine, said to be a son of Apollo, had daughters named for concepts like Health and Recuperation, and represents the healing side of the ancient medical arts — who is he?
Asclepius (Ancient) is a hero and god of medicine in ancient Greek religion and mythology.
He was the principal organizer of the 1963 March on Washington and a leader for civil rights, socialism, nonviolence, and gay rights — which activist is it?
Bayard Rustin (March 17, 1912 - August 24, 1987) was an American political activist and prominent leader in social movements for civil rights, socialism, nonviolence, and gay rights.
This Turkish statesman and poet served as prime minister four separate times between 1974 and 2002, chairing first the Republican People's Party and later his own Democratic Left Party — who is he?
Bülent Ecevit (28 May 1925 - 5 November 2006) was a Turkish statesman, poet, writer, scholar, and journalist.

This Republican engineer, whose father once served as New Hampshire governor and White House chief of staff, was himself elected governor of that state four times, matching only one predecessor. Who is he?
Chris Sununu (s-; born November 5, 1974) is an American politician and engineer who served as the 82nd governor of New Hampshire from 2017 to 2025.

The U.S. Navy's first-ever rear admiral, vice admiral, and admiral is remembered for a bold order at the Battle of Mobile Bay usually shortened to 'Damn the torpedoes ... full speed ahead.' Who was he?
Henri de La Tour d'Auvergne, Viscount of Turenne
David Farragut (also spelled Glascoe; July 5, 1801 - August 14, 1870) was a flag officer of the United States Navy during the American Civil War.
This New Zealand mountaineer, alongside Tenzing Norgay, became the first climber confirmed to reach the summit of Mount Everest, on 29 May 1953 — who is he?
Edmund Hillary (20 July 1919 - 11 January 2008) was a New Zealand mountaineer, explorer, and philanthropist.

Robert Cecil, Viscount Cecil of Chelwood
Ezra Meeker (December 29, 1830 - December 3, 1928) was an American pioneer who traveled the Oregon Trail by ox-drawn wagon as a young man, migrating from Iowa to the Pacific Coast.

Waged by Julius Caesar between 58 and 50 BC against the tribes of Gaul, this decade of Roman military campaigns culminated in the Battle of Alesia and the Republic's total conquest of the region. What conflict is this?
Gallic Wars were waged between 58 and 50 BC by the Roman general Julius Caesar against the peoples of Gaul (present-day France, Belgium, and Switzerland).

This Russian mystic and faith healer gained enormous influence over the imperial family of Tsar Nicholas II in the final years of the empire. Born a Siberian peasant in 1869, he's best remembered for his mysterious sway over the fate of Russia itself — who is this controversial figure?
Grigori Rasputin was Russian mystic (1869–1916). Grigori Yefimovich Rasputin (21 January [O.S. 9 January] 1869 – 30 December [O.S. 17 December] 1916) was a Russian mystic and faith healer.
FDR's vice president from 1941 to 1945, this Iowa-born agriculture and commerce secretary later ran for the White House as the new Progressive Party's nominee in 1948 — who was he?
Henry A. Wallace (October 7, 1888 - November 18, 1965) was the 33rd vice president of the United States, serving from 1941 to 1945, under President Franklin D. Roosevelt.

A Scottish politician born to Pakistani immigrant parents became the youngest justice secretary in 2018, then health secretary, before leading his party and nation from March 2023 to May 2024. Who served as First Minister of Scotland?
Humza Yousaf (born 7 April 1985) is a Scottish politician who served as First Minister of Scotland and Leader of the Scottish National Party (SNP) from March 2023 to May 2024.
An anti-apartheid fighter who spent ten years on Robben Island, this man rose to lead the ANC and then served as South Africa's president from 2009 to 2018 — who is he?
Jacob Zuma (born 12 April 1942) is a South African politician who served as the president of South Africa from 2009 to 2018.

This West Virginia politician served as secretary of state, then governor, then US senator over a 24-year span, remaining a Democrat until switching to independent in 2024; he also co-founded a coal brokerage company. Who is he?
Joe Manchin (born August 24, 1947) is an American politician and businessman from West Virginia.
Succeeding Rowan Williams in 2013, this archbishop presided over the wedding of Prince Harry and Meghan Markle during a tenure that saw the church's first female bishop ordained — who is he?
Justin Welby (born 6 January 1956) is a retired Anglican bishop who served as the 105th archbishop of Canterbury in the Church of England from 2013 to 2025.
A former transplant surgeon nicknamed 'Ko P,' this Taiwanese politician served as mayor of Taipei before founding his own political party. Who is he?
Ko Wen-je (pinyin: K Wnzh; born 6 August 1959), also known by his nickname Ko P, is a Taiwanese politician, physician, and transplant surgeon who served as the 13th mayor of Taipei from 2014 to 2022.
Relieved from her post by the Secretary of Defense in 2025, this admiral had been the first woman to serve as chief of naval operations and the first woman on the Joint Chiefs of Staff — who is she?

Lisa Franchetti (fran-; born 25 April 1964) is a retired United States Navy admiral who served as the 33rd chief of naval operations from 2 November 2023 to 21 February 2025, after being relieved by Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth.
After representing Florida in the Senate for over a decade, this Republican politician became the nation's top diplomat and acting national security advisor in 2025 — who is he?
Marco Rubio (born May 28, 1971) is an American politician, attorney, and diplomat serving as the 72nd United States secretary of state since 2025.

Ruling the Franks from the mid-5th century until Pepin the Short's takeover in 751, this dynasty defeated the Visigoths in 507 and the Burgundians in 534 to build Western Europe's most powerful realm — which dynasty?
Merovingian dynasty was the ruling family of the Franks from around the middle of the 5th century until Pepin the Short in 751.

This Indian independence activist and politician served as prime minister from 1977 to 1979 leading the Janata Party government, after decades holding posts from Bombay's chief ministership to deputy prime minister — who is he?
Prince Albert Victor, Duke of Clarence and Avondale

Morarji Desai (29 February 1896 - 10 April 1995) was an Indian politician and independence activist who served as the prime minister of India between 1977 and 1979 leading the government formed by the Janata Party.

This Florentine diplomat served Florence's republic while the Medici were out of power, then wrote a slim political treatise — unpublished until five years after his death — that earned him the title 'father of modern political science.' Who was he?
Niccolò Machiavelli (3 May 1469 - 21 June 1527) was a Florentine diplomat, author, philosopher, and historian who lived during the Italian Renaissance.
Backed by the Byzantine emperor Zeno, this Germanic people's king invaded Italy and preserved Roman law and administration from his capital at Ravenna — who were they?
Ostrogoths were a Roman-era Germanic people who, in the 5th and 6th centuries, established one of the two major Gothic kingdoms within the Western Roman Empire.
This former Dutch MP, who focused on tax and pension policy, stepped away from politics in 2025 citing burnout after founding the New Social Contract party — who is he?
Alfred, Duke of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha

Pieter Omtzigt (born 8 January 1974) is a Dutch former politician who served as a member of the House of Representatives between 2003 and 2025 apart from a short interruption between June and October 2010.
Chair of the Senate Homeland Security Committee, this Kentucky Republican ran for his party's presidential nomination in 2016 — who is he?
Rand Paul (born January 7, 1963) is an American politician serving as the junior United States senator from Kentucky since 2011.

In 1941 this Deputy to the Führer made a bizarre solo flight to Scotland hoping to talk Britain out of the war — and ended up a prisoner, later dying by suicide at 93 while still serving a life sentence. Who was he?
Rudolf Hess (He in German; 26 April 1894 - 17 August 1987) was a German politician, convicted war criminal, and a leading member of the Nazi Party in Germany.
An Old Bolshevik and Politburo member who led the Communist Party in Leningrad, he was gunned down at his office in 1934 — an assassination Stalin used to launch the Great Purge. Who was he?
Sergei Kirov (born Kostrikov; 27 March 1886 - 1 December 1934) was a Russian and Soviet politician and Bolshevik revolutionary.
Founded by crusading knights along the Baltic during the 13th-century Northern Crusades, this theocratic realm at its peak stretched from Prussia to Estonia and included Gotland — what was it called?
State of the Teutonic Order was a theocratic state located along the southeastern shore of the Baltic Sea in northern Europe.

This ancient Indo-European-speaking people inhabited large parts of Southeast Europe, in territory spanning modern Bulgaria, Romania, and northern Greece, as well as parts of northwestern Anatolia — who were they?
Thracians were an Indo-European-speaking people who inhabited large parts of Southeast Europe in ancient history. The Thracian culture emerged during the early Bronze Age, which began about 3500 BC.
This Argentine lawyer and conservative politician has served as her country's vice president since 2023, having founded a legal-studies center focused on terrorism victims. Who is she?
Victoria Villarruel (born 13 April 1975) is an Argentine politician, lawyer, writer, and activist who has served as the 38th vice president of Argentina since 2023.

Co-founder of the Center for Constitutional Rights and defender of the Chicago Seven, this attorney was dubbed by The New York Times 'the country's most controversial and, perhaps, its best-known lawyer.' Who?
William Kunstler (July 7, 1919 - September 4, 1995) was an American attorney and civil rights activist, known for defending the Chicago Seven.
Centered on the Avesta and the teachings of an ancient Iranian prophet, this faith — among the world's oldest organized religions — reveres a supreme deity named Ahura Mazda — name the religion?
Zoroastrianism is an Iranian religion centred on the Avesta and the teachings of Zarathushtra Spitama, who is more commonly referred to by the Greek translation, Zoroaster (Ancient).
Traditionally chanted by a muezzin from a mosque's minaret before each of the five daily prayers, what is this Islamic call known as?
Adhan: Islamic call to prayer. The five prayer times are known in Arabic as fajr (فجر), dhuhr (ظهر), asr (عصر), maghrib (مغرب), and isha (عشاء).
A criminal-law professor who earned his law degree at 24, this Peronist served as Argentina's longest-tenured Cabinet Chief before becoming the country's president from 2019 to 2023 — who is he?

Alberto Fernández: President of Argentina from 2019 to 2023. Born in Buenos Aires, Fernández attended the University of Buenos Aires, where he earned his law degree at age 24, and later became a professor of criminal law.
In 2024, this Manhattan district attorney became the first person to secure a criminal conviction of a former U.S. president — who is he?
Alvin Bragg: American lawyer and politician (born 1973)

Anne Boleyn: Queen of England from 1533 to 1536.

Assassination of Uthman: 656 murder of the third Rashidun caliph in Medina.

Hours after Vladimir Putin announced Russia's 'special military operation' on February 24, 2022, Russian airborne troops assaulted a strategic airfield near Kyiv, aiming to fly in reinforcements before being encircled and repelled by Ukrainian forces — which clash?
Battle of Antonov Airport: Part of the Russian invasion of Ukraine.
Nicknamed 'Kaka,' this politician served as the third Chief Minister of Chhattisgarh from 2018 to 2023 after years representing the Patan constituency — who is he?
"Keeper of greatness" was the meaning of his name — fitting for the 13th and final emperor of Vietnam's Nguyễn dynasty, who abdicated in August 1945 after Japan surrendered. Who was he?
Bảo Đại: Last emperor of Vietnam from 1926 to 1945 (1913–1997)

Fought between Bolivia and Paraguay from 1932 to 1935 over an oil-rich, semi-arid region also known for the thirst its soldiers suffered, this was the bloodiest 20th-century conflict in South America — what conflict is it?
Chaco War: War between Bolivia and Paraguay (1932 to 1935). The Chaco War (Spanish: Guerra del Chaco, Guarani: Cháko Ñorairõ) was fought from 1932 to 1935.

Democratic Republic of Afghanistan: Afghan state from 1978 to 1992.

Eadred: King of the English from 946 to 955.
Born under a different name and later adopting a new surname, this religious leader grew a small Detroit-based movement into a nationwide organization during the civil rights era — who is he?
Elijah Muhammad: African American religious leader (1897–1975)

Euroscepticism: Body of criticism of the European Union.

Five Star Movement: Italian political party. The Five Star Movement (Italian: Movimento 5 Stelle [moviˈmento ˈtʃiŋkwe ˈstelle], M5S) is a political party in Italy, led by Giuseppe Conte.
A former New Left activist at Meiji University, this Japanese writer founded a now-disbanded militant group that relocated to the Middle East in 1971 to pursue world revolution — who is she?
Fusako Shigenobu: Japanese communist activist. Born in Japan, Shigenobu became involved in New Left activism while attending night school at Meiji University in Tokyo.
Also known by two other names, this Israelite judge and prophet defeated the Midianites in the Hebrew Bible by leading just 300 men into battle — who is he?
Gideon: Character in the biblical Book of Judges.
This King of Sweden turned his country into a major European power during the Thirty Years' War, clinching a decisive win at the Battle of Breitenfeld in 1631 — who was he?
Gustavus Adolphus: King of Sweden from 1611 to 1632.
This ancient Egyptian sky goddess, linked to Horus and Ra, represented beauty, music, dance, and joy, while also serving as a vengeful protector known as the Eye of Ra — who is she?
Princess Alice of the United Kingdom
Hathor: Major goddess in ancient Egyptian religion.
Serving as Chief Minister of Assam since 2021, this politician switched from the Congress party to the BJP in 2015 and has represented Jalukbari in the state assembly six times — who is he?

Himanta Biswa Sarma: Chief Minister of Assam since 2021. Himanta Biswa Sarma (born 1 February 1969) is an Indian politician and lawyer serving as the 15th and the current Chief Minister of Assam since 2021.
Serving as prime minister across three separate periods spanning nearly four decades, this politician is Cambodia's longest-serving head of government — who is he?
Hun Sen: Prime Minister of Cambodia (1985–1993; 1998–2023)
Whose name means 'he will laugh,' this biblical patriarch was the son of Abraham and Sarah and the father of Jacob and Esau, living to age 180 — who was he?

Isaac: Biblical patriarch, son of Abraham and Sarah. Isaac first appears in the Torah, in which he is the son of Abraham and Sarah, the father of Jacob and Esau, and the grandfather of the twelve tribes of Israel.
Scottish-born to Irish parents, this socialist and union leader founded Ireland's first socialist party before being executed for his role in the 1916 Easter Rising. Who was he?
James Connolly: Irish republican, trade unionist and revolutionary (1868–1916)

An electrical engineer by training, he became the third paramount leader of China — serving as Communist Party general secretary from 1989 to 2002 — ranked among core leaders beside Mao, Deng, and Xi. Who was he?
Jiang Zemin: Leader of China from 1989 to 2002. Born in Yangzhou, Jiangsu, Jiang grew up during the years of Japanese occupation.
Sold into slavery in Egypt by his jealous brothers, this favored son of Jacob rose to become Pharaoh's second-in-command after correctly interpreting his dreams — who is he?
Joseph (Genesis): Biblical figure, son of Jacob and Rachel.
Estonia's first female prime minister, this politician resigned in 2024 to become the European Union's High Representative for Foreign Affairs — who is she?
Kaja Kallas: Estonian politician and diplomat (born 1977)

Surviving five assassination attempts and years of imprisonment and exile for his democratization activism, this opposition leader finally won election as South Korea's eighth president in 1997 — who is he?
Kim Dae-jung: President of South Korea from 1998 to 2003.
Recorded by the 12th-century chronicler Saxo as a Viking shield-maiden and onetime wife of the legendary Ragnar Lodbrok, this warrior may actually be rooted in myths about a Norse deity — who is she?
Lagertha: Legendary Viking shieldmaiden and ruler.
Ignited by 2011 protests in Benghazi, this North African conflict pitted rebels and their National Transitional Council against forces loyal to Colonel Gaddafi — what was it?
Libyan civil war (2011): 2011 armed conflict in North Africa.
The third son of a former Tamil Nadu chief minister, this DMK leader served as mayor of Chennai before becoming the state's chief minister himself in 2021 — who is he?

Mao Zedong: Leader of China from 1949 to 1976.
This Polish economist served as Prime Minister from 2017 to 2023 under the Law and Justice party, after earlier stints as both Finance Minister and Deputy Prime Minister. Who is he?

Mateusz Morawiecki: Prime Minister of Poland from 2017 to 2023. Mateusz Jakub Morawiecki (born 20 June 1968) is a Polish economist and politician who served as Prime Minister of Poland from 2017 to 2023.

Dubbed 'the greatest genius the early church ever produced,' which prolific 3rd-century theologian founded a school in Caesarea after starting his career in Alexandria?
Origen: Christian philosopher and theologian (c. 185 – c. 253)

A former primary school teacher and union leader who rose to prominence during a 2017 teachers' strike, this politician served as Peru's president until his failed self-coup in December 2022 — who is he?
Pedro Castillo: President of Peru from 2021 to 2022.
Once married to a future Roman emperor, this woman went on to become Nero's second wife, and a lavish excavated villa near Pompeii bears her name — who is she?
Poppaea Sabina: Roman empress from 62 to 65 AD.
A trained psychiatrist who became the first president of Republika Srpska, he spent twelve years as a fugitive before being convicted of genocide by a UN tribunal — who is he?

Grand Duchess Tatiana Nikolaevna of Russia

Named for a 1930s guerrilla leader who resisted US occupation, this Nicaraguan socialist party toppled the Somoza dynasty in 1979 and governed through the 1980s — which party?
Sandinista National Liberation Front: Nicaraguan socialist political party founded in 1961.

Sierra Leone Civil War: 1991–2002 war in West Africa.
Crowned in 1576 after marrying Queen Anna Jagiellon, this ruler defeated a rival claimant to become the third elected king of Poland — who was he?
Stephen Báthory: Ruler of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth from 1576 to 1586.

Punished in the underworld by standing in a pool beneath a fruit tree whose branches always pulled away from his grasp, this Greek mythological figure lent his name to the English word for teasing someone with something unreachable — who was he?
Tantalus: Greek mythological figure and son of Zeus.

Ukrainian People's Republic: 1917–18/1918–21 state in Eastern Europe.
Once governor of Donetsk Oblast, this pro-Russian politician served as Ukraine's fourth president until the 2014 Revolution of Dignity drove him into exile in Russia — who is he?
Viktor Yanukovych: President of Ukraine from 2010 to 2014.
A rags-to-riches Western Han general celebrated for his campaigns against the Xiongnu, he rose through ties to Emperor Wu and was uncle to the famed general Huo Qubing — who was he?

Władysław II Jagiełło: Grand Duke of Lithuania (1377–1434); King of Poland (1386–1434)
This Chinese politician led the Communist Party's anti-corruption watchdog from 2017 to 2022 before becoming chairman of the National People's Congress Standing Committee — who is he?
Who among these was born first?
Jabir ibn Hayyan (born 721) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these people was born first?
Patrick Geddes (born 1854) is the earliest of the four.
SQL (founded 1974) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four came first?
COBOL (founded 1959) is the earliest of the four.
Who among these is a physicist?
Louis Slotin is a physicist. Louis Alexander Slotin ( SLOHT-in; 1 December 1910 – 30 May 1946) was a Canadian physicist and chemist who took part in the Manhattan Project.
Pick the chemist from these four.
James Lovelock is a chemist. James Ephraim Lovelock (26 July 1919 – 26 July 2022) was an English independent scientist, environmentalist and futurist.
What is the atomic number of Unbiunium?
Unbiunium, also known as eka-actinium or element 121, is a hypothetical chemical element; it has symbol Ubu and atomic number 121.
In what year was J. Robert Oppenheimer born?
J. Robert Oppenheimer: In 1941, Oppenheimer was briefed about nuclear weapon design by Australian physicist Mark Oliphant.
In what year did Archimedes die?
Archimedes died during the siege of Syracuse, when he was killed by a Roman soldier despite orders that he should not be harmed.
In what year was Iron discovered?
Iron is a chemical element; it has symbol Fe (from Latin ferrum 'iron') and atomic number 26.
Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-25: Russian Aircraft Corporation MiG. Designed by the Soviet Union's Mikoyan-Gurevich bureau, it is an aircraft built primarily using stainless steel.
Which country is Sukhoi Su-57 from?
Sukhoi Su-57: Russia. The Sukhoi Su-57 (Russian: Сухой Су-57; NATO reporting name: Felon) is a twin-engine stealth multirole fighter aircraft developed by Sukhoi.
Who is credited with discovering Gaussian integral?
Gaussian integral: Leonhard Euler. The integral has a wide range of applications.
Who is credited with discovering Aspirin?
Aspirin: Raffaele Piria. Aspirin is used to treat inflammatory conditions including Kawasaki disease, pericarditis, and rheumatic fever.
Who is credited with discovering Boron?
Boron: Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac. Boron is a chemical element; it has symbol B and atomic number 5.

The active component of vinegar and the second simplest carboxylic acid, this colourless liquid with the formula CH₃COOH has been produced in large quantities since the third millennium BCE. What is this acid?
Acetic acid is an acidic, colourless liquid and organic compound with the chemical formula CH3COOH (also written as CH3CO2H, C2H4O2, or HC2H3O2).
A military pilot who became the first astronaut representing Turkey, he reached the International Space Station on 18 January 2024 aboard the Axiom Mission 3 flight — who is he?
Alper Gezeravcı (born 2 December 1979) is a military pilot and the first Turkish astronaut.
What term describes the discipline of measuring human body dimensions, applied everywhere from ergonomics and architecture to tracking historical living standards?
Anthropometry (from Ancient Greek (nthrpos) 'human' and (mtron) 'measure') refers to the measurement of the human individual.

Distinguished from celestial mechanics by asking what heavenly bodies ARE rather than where they are, this science applies physics and chemistry to the Sun, stars, galaxies, and exoplanets — which discipline?
Astrophysics is a science that applies the methods and principles of physics and chemistry in the study of astronomical objects and phenomena including the universe.
This steroid medication treats conditions ranging from rheumatoid arthritis and psoriasis to asthma, and is also given before preterm birth to help speed a baby's lung development — what drug is it?
Betamethasone is a steroid medication. It can be taken by mouth, injected into a muscle, or applied to the skin, typically in cream, lotion, or liquid forms.

Derived from Greek words for 'slow' and 'heart', this medical term describes a resting heart rate under 60 beats per minute — sometimes a red flag, sometimes just a sign of a well-conditioned athlete. Name the condition?
Bradycardia (brads), meaning "slow", and (karda), meaning "heart", also called bradyarrhythmia, is a resting heart rate under 60 beats per minute (BPM).
Caused by an overgrowth of a common yeast, this fungal infection is known as thrush when it affects the mouth and can also cause a genital yeast infection — name the condition?
Candidiasis is a fungal infection due to any species of yeasts in the genus Candida or those that were formerly classified in genus Candida but are now classified in the genus Candidozyma.
Despite no clinical evidence it treats any disease, this daisy-like plant is a staple in calming herbal tea, beer brewing, and even garden ground cover — what is it?
Chamomile (American English) or camomile (British English; see spelling differences) (or) is the common name for several daisy-like plants of the family Asteraceae.
Born near Toulouse, this French inventor is remembered chiefly as an aviation pioneer — though in 1870 he was also an early enthusiast of cycling in France; who was he?
Clément Ader (French; 2 April 1841 - 3 May 1925) was a French inventor and engineer who was born near Toulouse in Muret, Haute-Garonne, and died in Toulouse.
Going by puma, mountain lion, catamount, and panther depending on the region, this big cat is the most widely distributed wild land mammal in the Western Hemisphere — what is it?
Cougar (Puma concolor), also called puma, mountain lion, catamount, and panther, is a large feline native to the Americas.
Caused by either too little insulin or cells that ignore it, this condition keeps blood sugar stubbornly high and comes chiefly in a type 1 and a type 2 — what is it?
Diabetes is a group of common endocrine diseases characterized by sustained high blood sugar levels.
This social science examines the production, distribution, and consumption of goods and services, analyzing everything from individual agents to entire economies. What discipline is this?
Economics is a social science that studies the production, distribution, and consumption of goods and services.
This class of mental health condition is defined by an enduring, pervasive pattern of behavior, emotion, and thought that deviates from social norms and develops early in life. What is it?
Erythritol is an organic compound, the naturally occurring achiral meso four-carbon sugar alcohol (or polyol).
Which evergreen conifer genus has needle-like leaves attached singly to the branch by a circular base, and cones that stand upright like a cedar's rather than hanging down? What is it?
Fir are evergreen coniferous trees belonging to the genus Abies in the family Pinaceae.
Native to Pacific coastal waters from Alaska to Baja California, this giant burrowing clam can grow a siphon over three feet long and live for more than a century — which creature?
Geoduck (Panopea generosa) is a species of very large saltwater clam in the family Hiatellidae.

These common coastal seabirds, most closely related to terns and skimmers, were once known by an older name still surviving in some English dialects and cognate with the German word Möwe — what birds are they?
Gull (see Taxonomy), are seabirds of the subfamily Larinae.
First identified in 1910, this organic compound is stored in mast cells and basophils and, though not made by classic endocrine glands, still acts as a local hormone — what compound is it?
Histamine is an organic nitrogenous compound found in mammals and many vegetables, fruits and food products.

For decades this University of Virginia psychiatrist ran a Division of Perceptual Studies and gathered evidence that memories — and even bodily features — might carry across lives. Which researcher into reincarnation was he?

Ian Stevenson (October 31, 1918 - February 8, 2007) was a Canadian-born American psychiatrist, the founder and director of the Division of Perceptual Studies at the University of Virginia School of Medicine.

This American scientist co-authored a landmark 1953 paper with Francis Crick proposing the double-helix structure of DNA, building on research by Rosalind Franklin, and shared a 1962 Nobel Prize for the discovery — who is he?
James Watson (April 6, 1928 - November 6, 2025) was an American molecular biologist, geneticist, and zoologist.

Sharing the 1973 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, this ethologist was among the first to decode the honey bee's waggle dance — a theory greeted with such skepticism that it took decades to be vindicated. Who was he?
Karl von Frisch (20 November 1886 - 12 June 1982) was a German-Austrian ethologist who received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1973, along with Nikolaas Tinbergen and Konrad Lorenz.

This Hungarian-born physicist conceived the nuclear chain reaction in 1933, drafted the famous letter Einstein signed to launch the Manhattan Project, then later petitioned President Truman not to drop the bomb on civilians — who was he?

Leo Szilard (born Le Spitz; February 11, 1898 - May 30, 1964) was a Hungarian-born American physicist, biologist and inventor who made numerous important discoveries in nuclear physics and the biological sciences.
Reclassified in 2021 as part of the order Psocodea alongside booklice and barklice, these tiny wingless parasites cement their eggs to a single host for life — what are they called?
Louse (pl.: lice) is the common name for any member of the infraorder Phthiraptera, which contains nearly 5,000 species of wingless parasitic insects.
Google's employee No. 20 and its first woman software engineer, she later left to run a famous internet company as CEO from 2012 until Verizon bought it — who is she?
Marissa Mayer (born May 30, 1975) is an American business executive, software engineer, and investor who served as president and chief executive officer of Yahoo!
What neurological disorder causes moderate-to-severe, often one-sided headaches, frequently accompanied by nausea, light and sound sensitivity, and sometimes preceded by a sensory 'aura'?
Migraine is a neurological disorder that causes moderate-to-severe headaches. The pain usually affects one side of the head.
With somewhere between 66 and 70 species across nine subfamilies, this carnivore family stretches from tiny weasels all the way up to the wolverine. What is it?
Mustelidae (from Latin mustela, weasel) are a diverse family of carnivoran mammals, including weasels, badgers, otters, sea otters, polecats, martens, grisons and wolverines.

Considered primary if a child has never had a long dry stretch, this common childhood condition — usually a developmental delay rather than an illness — is commonly called bedwetting. What's its clinical name?
Nocturnal enuresis (NE), also informally called bedwetting, is involuntary urination while asleep after the age at which bladder control usually begins.
Derived from an ancient Roman unit called the uncia, this unit of mass equals 1/16 of a pound in its common form, though a heavier 'troy' version weighs precious metals — name the unit?
Ounce is any of several different units of mass, weight, or volume and is derived almost unchanged from the uncia, an Ancient Roman unit of measurement.

This short-acting barbiturate is used as a sedative and anticonvulsant in low doses, but in high doses causes fatal respiratory arrest, making it a drug of choice for both veterinary euthanasia and U.S. executions — what is it?
Pentobarbital (US) or pentobarbitone (British and Australian) is a short-acting barbiturate typically used as a sedative, a preanesthetic, and to control convulsions in emergencies.
Native to Eurasia and identifiable by short, blue-green needles, this member of the pine family goes by several regional common names — name the species (Latin binomial)?
Pinus sylvestris is a species of tree in the pine family Pinaceae that is native to Eurasia.
Split into the strepsirrhines — lemurs and lorisids — and the haplorhines — tarsiers, monkeys and apes — this order ranges in size down to tiny Madame Berthe's — what is it?

Primate is an order of mammals, which is further divided into the strepsirrhines, which include lemurs, galagos, and lorisids; and the haplorhines, which include tarsiers and simians (monkeys and apes).

Founding an organization promoting swadeshi economics against globalization, this Indian social activist later allied with a yoga guru to combine that economic message with the promotion of yoga and Ayurveda — who is he?
Rajiv Dixit (30 November 1967 - 30 November 2010) was an Indian social activist who founded the Azadi Bachao Andolan.

This English X-ray crystallographer's photographs were crucial to unraveling the structure of DNA, yet her contribution went largely unrecognized in her lifetime, earning her posthumous nicknames like "the wronged heroine" — who was she?
Rosalind Franklin (25 July 1920 - 16 April 1958) was an English chemist and X-ray crystallographer.
With segmented bony armor, an upright posture, and a curling prehensile tail, these 46 species of tiny bony fish are cousins to the pipefishes and seadragons — what are they?
Seahorse (also written sea-horse and sea horse) is any of 46 species of small marine bony fish in the genus Hippocampus.
Once placed alone in the genus Uncia before phylogenetics moved it into Panthera, this high-altitude cat ranges across the Tibetan Plateau and Himalayas — what is it?
Snow leopard (Panthera uncia) is a species of large cat in the genus Panthera of the family Felidae.
Lacking the powder down that herons and ibises use to clean off fish slime, these bill-clattering wading birds come in 20 living species across six genera — which birds?
Stork are large, long-legged, long-necked wading birds with long, stout bills.

Equal to one weber per square metre, this SI unit of magnetic flux density was adopted in 1960 and named for a Serbian-American electrical engineer, on the proposal of a Slovenian engineer — name this unit?
Tesla (unit) (symbol: T) is the unit of magnetic flux density (B) (also called magnetic B-field) in the International System of Units (SI).
Roughly eight times more potent than an older analogue, this bleeding-control medication is also prescribed for hereditary angioedema — what is it?
Tranexamic acid is a medication used to treat or prevent excessive blood loss from major trauma, postpartum bleeding, surgery, tooth removal, nosebleeds, and heavy menstruation.
This British-American structural biologist shared the 2009 Nobel in Chemistry for revealing the ribosome's structure and later led the Royal Society as president — who is he?
Venki Ramakrishnan (born 1952) is a British-American structural biologist.
Marketed under names like Rompun, this veterinary sedative and alpha-2 adrenergic agonist is often combined with ketamine for animal anesthesia and used as an emetic in cats — what is it?

Xylazine is a structural analog of clonidine and an 2-adrenergic receptor agonist, sold under many trade names worldwide, most notably the Bayer brand name Rompun, as well as Anased, Sedazine and Chanazine.
Caused by a mutation in the FGFR3 gene, this genetic disorder is the most common cause of short stature, marked by shortened limbs, a normal-length torso and a prominent forehead — what is it called?
Achondroplasia: Genetic condition, the most common form of dwarfism.
With wingspans reaching up to eleven and a half feet, which large seabird family ranges across the Southern Ocean and North Pacific but is absent from the North Atlantic?
Albatross: Family of large seabirds. The albatrosses are usually regarded as falling into four genera, but disagreement exists over the number of species.
The heaviest member of its family, this Southeastern U.S. reptile sees males stretch up to 15 feet and tip 1,000 pounds — and it's the larger of just two surviving species in its genus. What is it?
American alligator: Crocodilian native to the Southeastern United States.

Characterized by extreme food restriction and a fear of gaining weight despite being underweight, this eating disorder is described in the DSM-5 as involving a disturbance in how one perceives their own body shape — what's the condition called?
Anorexia nervosa: Eating disorder. Individuals with anorexia nervosa have a fear of gaining weight, despite the fact that they are typically underweight.
Sold under the brand name Abilify, this atypical antipsychotic treats schizophrenia, bipolar mania, and irritability linked to autism spectrum disorder — what is it?
Aripiprazole: Atypical antipsychotic medication. Aripiprazole is taken by mouth or via injection into a muscle.
Delivered to the RAF starting in 1956, this delta-wing strategic bomber was considered the most advanced but riskiest of Britain's three V bombers — which aircraft?
Avro Vulcan: British jet-powered delta wing strategic bomber.
A largely self-taught naturalist and astronomer born to a free mother in Maryland, he helped survey the District of Columbia and corresponded with Thomas Jefferson — who was he?
Benjamin Banneker: American scientist, surveyor and farmer (1731–1806)
Despite being just 12 to 20 cm long, this small marine creature's vivid markings flash brighter when it feels threatened, and its bite delivers a neurotoxin called tetrodotoxin — what is it?
Blue-ringed octopus: Four species of mollusk.

Unique among mammals, human females are the only ones to permanently develop this secondary sex organ at puberty rather than just during pregnancy, and it later produces milk via the mammary gland — which body part?
Breast: Part of the female primate torso that has mammary glands.
With the formula CaC2, this industrial compound reacts with trace moisture to give off a garlicky smell and is used to generate acetylene gas in old-fashioned lamps — what is it?
Calcium carbide: Chemical compound. Its main use industrially is in the production of acetylene and calcium cyanamide.
This mammalian order of flesh-eating species is split into cat-like and dog-like suborders, Feliformia and Caniformia, and ranks as the sixth-largest order of mammals — which order?
Carnivora: Order of mammals. Carnivora ( kar-NIV-ər-ə) is an order of placental mammals specialised primarily in eating flesh, whose members are formally referred to as carnivorans.
Known in North America as fireweed and in Britain as rosebay willowherb, this perennial flowering plant thrives across the boreal forests of the Northern Hemisphere — which plant?
Chamaenerion angustifolium: Species of flowering plant in the willowherb family.
This fluoroquinolone antibiotic treats everything from typhoid fever to urinary tract infections but can rarely cause tendon rupture — what drug?
Ciprofloxacin: Fluoroquinolone antibiotic. Ciprofloxacin, sold under the brand name Cipro among others, is a fluoroquinolone antibiotic used to treat a number of bacterial infections.

Nicknamed 'flying lemurs' despite not being lemurs at all, these Southeast Asian gliding mammals are primates' closest living relatives and belong to an order whose name means 'skin wing' — what are they called?
Going by puma, mountain lion, catamount, and panther depending on where you stand, this big cat is the most widely distributed wild land mammal in the Americas — what is it?
Cougar: Wild cat species native to the Americas.
Native to Mexico and Central America, this tuberous flowering plant blooms in nearly every hue except blue, and its tubers store energy as inulin rather than starch — what is it?
Dahlia: Genus of flowering plants in the daisy family Asteraceae.
Approved for medical use in the US back in 1950, this medication treats intestinal spasms such as those seen in irritable bowel syndrome — what is it called?
Nicknamed 'Viking disease,' this hand condition — first surgically treated in 1831 by the surgeon it's named after — permanently curls the ring finger inward. What is it?
Dupuytren's contracture: Medical condition featuring permanent bending of fingers.

The heaviest aircraft ever built by its Brazilian manufacturer, this twin-engine jet transport was developed as a derivative of a regional jetliner, similar in role to the C-130 Hercules. Which aircraft?
Embraer C-390 Millennium: Brazilian military transport aircraft/tanker.
The simplest alkene and the most-produced organic compound on Earth, this colorless gas is also a natural plant hormone used to ripen fruit — what is it?
This principle describes how a changing magnetic field generates an electric current, underpinning the operation of transformers, generators, and motors — what is it called?
Faraday's law of induction: Basic law of electromagnetism.
The lightest halogen, this pale yellow gas is so reactive that several 19th-century chemists died or were injured trying to isolate it, until Henri Moissan finally succeeded in 1886 — which element?
Fluorine: Chemical element with atomic number 9 (F)
Tucked beneath the liver, this pear-shaped organ stores and concentrates bile before releasing it to aid fat digestion in the small intestine — which organ?
Gallbladder: Organ in humans and other vertebrates.
The tallest land animal alive and the largest ruminant on Earth, its closest living relative is the okapi — which long-necked African mammal is it?

Once classified as a subfamily of the seabasses, this diverse family of marine ray-finned fish is now treated as distinct, with most members drawn from two large genera. What are they commonly called?
Grouper: Family of fishes. The common name "grouper" is usually given to fish in one of two large genera: Epinephelus and Mycteroperca.
Nicknamed bindwood or lovestone, this clinging evergreen native to Europe scales tree trunks, walls, and fences — which plant?
Hedera helix: Species of flowering plant.

Widely credited as the 'father of the Indian nuclear programme,' this theoretical physicist founded the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research and chaired India's first Atomic Energy Commission — who is it?
Homi J. Bhabha: Indian nuclear physicist (1909–1966)
It usually causes no symptoms at all, yet this persistently elevated arterial pressure is a leading cause of stroke, heart failure and premature death worldwide — what's the medical name for it?
Hypertension: Long-term high blood pressure in the arteries.

Marked by an IQ below 70 and deficits in everyday adaptive skills first apparent in childhood, this neurodevelopmental condition was formerly called 'mental retardation' in the U.S. — what is it now called?
A French soldier turned naturalist, this early proponent of biological evolution published the three-volume 'Flore françoise' and joined the French Academy of Sciences in 1779 — who is he?
Nicknamed 'Iron Annie,' which corrugated-skin transport plane began life as a 1930 civilian airliner before Nazi Germany converted it for military use?
Situated between two larger folds of skin, these paired flaps extend from the inner vaginal and urethral openings and form the clitoral hood above — which structures are these?
Labia minora: Flaps of skin on either side of the vaginal opening in the vulva.
Cell signaling, homeostasis, metabolism, growth and reproduction are its hallmarks — and every instance of it eventually reaches death. What capacity in matter is this?

This Canadian physicist worked on the Manhattan Project determining critical mass values for uranium and plutonium, and in 1946 was fatally exposed to radiation in a lab accident at Los Alamos — who is he?
Louis Slotin: Canadian physicist and chemist (1910–1946)
Nicknamed sea cows, these slow-moving herbivorous mammals graze on more than 60 kinds of aquatic plants in the Caribbean, the Amazon basin, and West Africa — what are they?
Manatee: Genus of mammals. The main causes of death for manatees are human-related issues, such as habitat destruction and human objects.
This cone-shaped part of the brainstem controls involuntary functions from sneezing to heart rate, and was once known simply as 'the bulb' — which structure?
Medulla oblongata: Structure of the brain stem.
This branch of economics studies how individual firms and consumers allocate scarce resources, as opposed to the economy-wide view of its counterpart — which field?
Microeconomics: Behavior of individuals and firms.
The platypus and the four species of echidna are the only living mammals in this order that lay eggs rather than bear live young — what is it called?

Dropped from a B-52 and boosted by a modified Pegasus rocket stage before its own scramjet took over, this experimental hypersonic craft still holds the record for fastest jet-powered flight at about Mach 9.6 — what is it?
NASA X-43: Unmanned US experimental hypersonic aircraft, 1991-2000.

Named for a mythological daughter of Tantalus, this silvery transition metal with atomic number 41 was once called columbium and is now prized as a nickel-free option in hypoallergenic jewelry — which element?
Niobium: Chemical element with atomic number 41 (Nb)
Born in Nishapur during the Seljuk era, this Persian polymath solved general cubic equations using intersecting conic sections centuries before Descartes — who was he?
Omar Khayyam: Persian polymath and poet (1048–1131)
A perennial herb from the mountains of East Asia, its root is the original source of a famous herbal supplement — though studies find little evidence it actually works. Which plant?
Panax ginseng: Species of flowering plant.
Almost every member of this flightless, countershaded clan sticks to the Southern Hemisphere — except one lone species that creeps up to the equator in the Galapagos. What bird is it?
Penguin: Family of aquatic flightless birds.
Plants, algae, and cyanobacteria run this light-powered process, splitting water to release oxygen as a byproduct while banking energy in sugars like glucose. What is it called?
Photosynthesis: Biological process to convert light into chemical energy.
This birth defect results in one or more extra fingers or toes and has been linked to at least 39 different genetic mutations — what is it called?
Polydactyly: Physical anomaly involving extra fingers or toes.
Native to Eurasia and known by the common names 'cherry plum' and 'myrobalan plum,' this species is thought to be a parent of the cultivated plum — what is it, scientifically?
Prunus cerasifera: Species of plum. Native to Eurasia and naturalized elsewhere, P. cerasifera is believed to be one of the parents of the cultivated plum.
Built from bases including uracil, adenine, guanine, and cytosine, this molecule can serve as a template for building proteins or catalyze reactions itself — what is it?
RNA: Family of large biological molecules.
One of the largest land megafauna left, this odd-toed ungulate has five surviving species — two in Africa, three across South and Southeast Asia — and a name meaning "nose-horned." What is it?
Discovered in 1844 by Karl Ernst Claus and named in honor of Russia, which unreactive platinum-group element with atomic number 44 now caps extreme ultraviolet photomasks for chip lithography?
Ruthenium: Chemical element with atomic number 44 (Ru)
Nicknamed 'Devil's Breath' and derived from nightshade plants, which motion-sickness drug has also been used historically as a deliriant?
Resembling a long-nosed mouse but actually a closer relative of hedgehogs and moles, this small mammal has sharp spike-like teeth rather than gnawing incisors — what is it?
Also called the mountain-ash despite not being a true ash, this rose-family tree grows small red berries beloved by birds — which species?
Sorbus aucuparia: Species of flowering plant in the rose family Rosaceae.
Sitting between the esophagus and the small intestine, this muscular organ uses acid and enzymes to chemically break down food, giving us the word 'gastric' — which organ?
Stomach: Digestive organ. The stomach is a muscular, hollow organ in the upper gastrointestinal tract of humans and many other animals, including several invertebrates.
Sold under the brand name Cialis, this erectile dysfunction medication can remain effective for up to 36 hours after a single dose — which drug?
Tadalafil: Medication used to treat erectile dysfunction.
This Hungarian-American aerospace pioneer made crucial advances in supersonic and hypersonic airflow, and the agreed boundary of outer space — the "___ line" — bears his name. Who was he?
Theodore von Kármán: Hungarian-American mathematician, aerospace engineer and physicist (1881–1963)
Marketed as Topamax, this oral medication treats epilepsy and prevents migraines, though it can cause weight loss and kidney stones as side effects — what is it?
Topiramate: Medication used to treat epilepsy and migraine.
Spread by body lice, chiggers, or fleas depending on the strain, this group of bacterial diseases causes fever, headache, and rash, and is treated with the antibiotic doxycycline — what is it?
Typhus: Group of infectious diseases. Typhus, also known as typhus fever, is a group of infectious diseases that include epidemic typhus, scrub typhus, and murine typhus.
Despite a scientific name meaning 'sand burrower,' this snake actually prefers rocky terrain and is considered Europe's most dangerous viper thanks to fangs up to 13mm long — which species?
Vipera ammodytes: Species of snake. It is reputed to be the most dangerous of the European vipers due to its large size, long fangs (up to 13 mm) and high venom toxicity.

By measuring weak natural radioactivity with sensitive Geiger counters, this American chemist developed a dating method in 1949 that revolutionized archaeology — and won him a 1960 Nobel Prize. Who was he?
Known on the street as a date-rape drug but used medically to treat narcolepsy and cataplexy, this natural neurotransmitter is also a precursor to GABA in the brain — what compound is it?

Γ-Hydroxybutyric acid: Chemical compound. γ-Hydroxybutyric acid, also known as gamma-hydroxybutyric acid, GHB, or 4-hydroxybutanoic acid, is a naturally occurring neurotransmitter and a depressant drug.
Berkelium is denoted by which symbol?
The symbol for berkelium is Bk. Berkelium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Bk and atomic number 97.

In what year was Sigourney Weaver born?
Sigourney Weaver: Susan Alexandra "Sigourney" Weaver ( sig-OR-nee; born October 8, 1949) is an American actress.
In what year was Michael Keaton born?
Michael Keaton: Michael John Douglas (born September 5, 1951), known professionally as Michael Keaton, is an American actor.
In what year was Eva Mendes born?
Eva Mendes: Eva de la Caridad Méndez (Spanish: [ˈeβa ðe la kaɾiˈðað ˈmendes]; born March 5, 1974), known professionally as Eva Mendes, is an American former actress.
In what year was Zooey Deschanel born?
Zooey Deschanel: Zooey Claire Deschanel (born January 17, 1980) is an American actress and singer.
In what year was David Tennant born?
David Tennant: David John Tennant (né McDonald; born 18 April 1971) is a Scottish actor.
In what year was Linda Cardellini born?
Linda Cardellini: Linda Edna Cardellini (born June 25, 1975) is an American actress.
In what year was Scott Adkins born?
Scott Adkins: Scott Edward Adkins (born 17 June 1976) is an English actor and martial artist.
In what year was Kevin Bacon born?
Kevin Bacon: Kevin Norwood Bacon (born July 8, 1958) is an American actor.
In what year was Song Kang born?
Song Kang (Korean: 송강; born April 23, 1994) is a South Korean actor.
In what year was Patrick Swayze born?
Patrick Swayze: Patrick Wayne Swayze ( SWAY-zee; August 18, 1952 – September 14, 2009) was an American actor, singer-songwriter and dancer.
In what year was Paul Reubens born?
Paul Reubens: Reubens developed his Pee-wee character at the Groundlings.
In what year did Truman Capote die?
Truman Capote: Capote had a troubled childhood caused by his parents' divorce, a long absence from his mother, and multiple moves.
